rationale: In this app's BSB the two verses do not look alike in English: Genesis 18:14 reads 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' and Luke 1:37 reads 'For no word from God will ever fail.' The link is in the Greek. The Septuagint of Genesis 18:14 (Blue Letter Bible text) reads 'μὴ ἀδυνατεῖ παρὰ τῷ θεῷ ῥῆμα'; Luke 1:37 in Nestle 1904 and Westcott-Hort reads 'ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα'. Both use the same verb (ἀδυνατέω, 'be impossible'), the same preposition with 'God', and the same noun ῥῆμα ('word' or 'thing'). The Expositor's Greek Testament gives the verb's New Testament uses as 'here and in Matthew 17:20'. The differences are real: Luke's verb is future, not present; Luke adds 'every' (πᾶν); and the critical texts have 'God' in the genitive ('from God'), which the Expositor's Greek Testament says 'seems to demand' the rendering 'no word of God shall be weak', the sense the BSB follows (but Field, adopting the same reading, translates 'for from God no word (or no thing) shall be impossible'), while the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus have the dative 'with God', as the Septuagint does. The setting also matches: in Luke 1:36 the angel cites Elizabeth, who 'has conceived a son in her old age' and 'was called barren', just as Genesis 18:11 says Sarah 'had passed the age of childbearing'. Named commentators draw the link: the Cambridge Bible on Genesis 18:14 says the Septuagint wording 'finds an echo in St Luke 1:37'; the Pulpit Commentary on 18:14 compares Luke 1:37; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Luke 1:37 calls it 'referring to what was said by the angel to Abraham in like case (Ge 18:14)'; Bengel quotes the Septuagint of 18:14 under Luke 1:37. Graded allusion, not quotation, because Luke has no citation formula and does not name Abraham or Sarah. Graded strong because the shared Greek wording is specific, the narrative situation (an angel, a barren and aged woman, a promised son) matches, and several named commentators make the link; it is not graded explicit because Luke never says it is pointing back.
